result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.trav_both()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Traverse from selected nodes to all neighbors. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21161-L21238){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.trav_both() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Bidirectional traversal](/assets/graphs/trav-both.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: in a seven-node directed graph, node C is selected (accent). Right: after trav_both() the selection is every node one edge away from C in either direction, A, B, D, and E; C itself and the more distant F and G are not selected." width="100%"} Moves the node selection one step along the edges of the graph, ignoring direction: the new selection is every node adjacent to at least one currently selected node, whether through an outgoing or an incoming edge. The current node selection is *replaced*, not extended. Traversals let you walk the graph with the selection as a cursor, which is useful for: - finding the direct neighbors of a group of nodes in one step, then acting on them with a `*_ws` method - exploring a directed graph as if it were undirected, e.g., everything that a node either depends on or is depended on by - building multi-step walks by chaining with `trav_out()` and `trav_in()` Because the selection is replaced, the starting nodes are only kept if they are themselves adjacent to another selected node (or have a self-loop). To keep the starting nodes as well, use `select_nodes_in_neighborhood(mode="all")` instead, which adds the k-hop neighborhood to the existing selection. In an undirected graph this behaves exactly like `trav_out()` and `trav_in()`. If no nodes are selected, nothing happens. The edge selection is not affected. The graph is modified in place and returned for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The same graph (modified in place) for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Starting from "B" and traversing both directions reaches both of its neighbors, "A" and "C", even though both edges point *into* "B". "B" itself is no longer selected: ::: {#eb36e26e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) graph.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")]) node_b_id = graph.get_id_from_label("B") graph.select_nodes_by_id([node_b_id]).trav_both() sorted(graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.get_selected_node_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'C'] ``` ::: ::: By contrast, `trav_out()` from "B" would find nothing, since "B" has no outgoing edges. Starting from several nodes, the result is the union of their neighbors. Here "A" and "B" are adjacent, so each ends up in the other's neighbor set and both stay selected, along with "C": ::: {#e5b9daf3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) seeds = [path.get_id_from_label("A"), path.get_id_from_label("B")] path.select_nodes_by_id(seeds).trav_both() sorted(path.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in path.get_selected_node_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C'] ``` ::: :::
